summary: Reports on a workshop about Internet privacy held in December 2010 by the IAB with the W3C, the Internet Society and MIT. Participants found it hard to design, deploy and analyze privacy-protecting protocols and suggested possible next steps. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Smart people met for two days to talk about keeping your information private online. This is the meeting write-up, listing the hard parts and ideas for what to do next.

subtitle: How the Internet community approaches privacy in technical standards.

tldr.problem: The Internet standards community lacks a systematic understanding of how to design protocols and systems that protect user privacy.
tldr.mechanism: In 2010, the IAB organized a multi-day workshop with the W3C, ISOC, and MIT CSAIL to identify the core design and deployment challenges in privacy-protecting systems.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified fingerprinting, information leakage, transparency gaps, and misaligned incentives as key obstacles, and proposed next steps for both the IETF and W3C to advance privacy awareness in standards development.

today: RFC 6462 is an Informational RFC and has not been superseded. It remains the foundational documentation of the Internet community's privacy challenges and serves as a reference point for privacy work in standards organizations.

sections.title: Internet Privacy at Standards Level
sections.content:
RFC 6462 documents the 2010 Internet Privacy Workshop, a two-day event in December 2010 hosted by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in partnership with the W3C, the Internet Society (ISOC), and MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). The workshop brought together about 80 technical experts, policymakers, and researchers to understand how Internet-based systems can be designed to respect privacy, and what specific work the IETF and W3C could undertake.

The core challenge the workshop addressed: privacy concerns now appear across the Internet—at the network layer, in web browsers, and in data-sharing platforms—yet Internet standards organizations have no systematic approach to anticipating, designing for, or evaluating privacy. Unlike security, which gained organizational infrastructure in the IETF over decades, privacy remained fragmented.
sections.plainLanguage: Many different people who work on Internet technology met to figure out how to make the Internet more private. They talked about what makes it hard to keep people's information secret.

sections.title: Core Design Challenges in Privacy Systems
sections.content:
The workshop surfaced five foundational design challenges that recur across protocols and applications:

Fingerprinting: Internet protocols and applications share so many unique identifiers (IP addresses, cookies, browser features, hardware parameters) that remote nodes can create a unique fingerprint of a user's device or behavior and track them over time. This is hard to prevent because many identifiers exist for legitimate reasons, not tracking.

Information leakage: Protocols leak sensitive data in unintended ways. For example, HTTP referrer headers expose the URI of the page that sent the user to a site, inadvertently revealing search terms or user IDs embedded in URLs.

First vs. third parties: The distinction between a site the user directly requested and content embedded from elsewhere is technically simple (based on domain matching) but does not match user expectations, making it hard to provide meaningful controls.

Lack of transparency: Users rarely understand what data is collected, how it is used, or what the tradeoffs are. Privacy policies are lengthy, complex, and infrequently read. Even visual signals (like targeted ads) often pass unnoticed.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping secrets on the Internet is hard. Websites can recognize you by lots of tiny clues. Private information gets mixed into web addresses. It is hard to tell the difference between the main website and hidden trackers. And people do not know what information is being collected about them.

sections.title: Deployment and Incentive Barriers
sections.content:
Even if protocols include privacy features, deploying them at scale faces three barriers:

Generative protocols vs. contextual threats: Generic protocols like HTTP or TCP are used in countless scenarios with different privacy threats. Protocol designers cannot foresee every deployment context. A feature that defends against one threat may be useless or harmful in another. IPv6 privacy extensions protect against MAC-address-based tracking but do not prevent ISP-level tracking.

Privacy vs. usability: Strong privacy protections often exact a usability cost. Tor provides strong anonymity but slows browsing and breaks plug-ins and JavaScript. Blocking HTTP referrer headers improves privacy but may break site personalization. Users often do not understand these tradeoffs, and implementors must choose whether to sacrifice privacy or features.

Business and regulatory incentives: Many web services are funded by advertising or data sale. Companies have little economic incentive to limit data collection. Regulation can shift these incentives, but uneven or absent regulatory pressure leaves companies free to track. P3P, an earlier attempt to let sites express privacy policies in machine-readable form, failed partly because sites had no incentive to implement it honestly.
sections.plainLanguage: Making privacy work is hard because one solution does not fit all situations. Strong privacy can be annoying to use. And many companies make money from collecting data, so they do not want to stop.

sections.title: Next Steps for Standards Organizations
sections.content:
The IETF and W3C were identified as key organizations to advance privacy-aware standards:

For the IETF, participants proposed: (1) creating a privacy directorate to review Internet-Drafts for privacy implications, drawing on the model of the security directorate; (2) developing guidance on privacy considerations for protocol developers, similar to existing security guidance; and (3) exploring technical challenges in fingerprinting and anonymized routing.

For the W3C, proposals included: forming a privacy interest group; developing guidance on fingerprinting and referrer-header leakage in web specs; addressing data minimization in web APIs; integrating usability considerations into specifications; and considering privacy for non-browser protocols.

Both organizations acknowledged that privacy consciousness, like security consciousness, must evolve from ad-hoc efforts into systematic practice, with tools, training, and expert review embedded in the standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop said that standards organizations should have special reviewers looking at privacy, the way they already have people checking security. They should write down how to design for privacy. And the web standards group should think about fingerprinting and how much information websites can see.

sections.title: Impact and Status
sections.content:
RFC 6462 is a workshop report, not a standards specification. Its role is to document the consensus findings of a key group of privacy experts and offer guidance for standards work. While it does not mandate action, it framed the privacy agenda in IETF and W3C for over a decade.

The IETF did create a privacy directorate, as proposed. The W3C formed privacy groups and pursued several of the recommended tracks (Do Not Track, referrer policy, privacy considerations for specs). However, the broader challenge—systematic privacy consciousness in Internet standards—remains ongoing, and many of the core tensions identified in 2010 (privacy vs. usability, privacy vs. business incentives) persist.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a report on the workshop, not a new rule. It told standards groups to work harder on privacy. Some of what the report suggested has happened; some has not.
